extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants / investigators preparing submissions or resubmissions
extracted.subtask_short: NIH grant cover letter & conflict strategy
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for NIH applicants on crafting cover letters, requesting study section/IC assignment, and preempting or excluding conflicted reviewers when submitting or resubmitting grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short, focused cover letter requesting study section and IC
rubrics_metrics.description: “I ask that this be reviewed by GRZLLP study section because [insert buzzwords that overlap between your application and the CSR official description of the study section]. I also request that it be assigned to [insert your favorite IC] because of blumbelty mumble obvious reasons”. That’s it. Short and to the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the cover letter brief; use buzzwords that match the CSR study section description to justify assignment; give concise reasons for IC choice. Avoid long narrative here — the goal is routing/assignment, not argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: List conflicted reviewers (to be excluded) in the cover letter with reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation (from an OER podcast cited): list conflicted reviewers who you wish not to review your grant right in your cover letter. With the reason for the conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a credible reason for each alleged conflict. Several commenters (including a Scientific Review Officer) state that SROs will eliminate anyone the applicant lists as a conflict if a credible reason is provided. Be factual — vague accusations like 'hates me' are inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do NOT list suggested reviewers by name in the cover letter (NIH warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: “NEVER, EVER, EVER list the names of people you might ‘suggest’ to review it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An SRO warns that naming suggested reviewers will practically guarantee those people will NOT be asked to review your application. Agency norms differ (see separate metric on agency differences), so do not confuse journal practice with NIH practice. If you want to propose reviewers, contact PO/SRO directly first or follow explicit agency guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact program officer and SRO before submission to secure assignment assent
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to talk/e-mail to a program officer and scientific review officer and gain their assent that your application should be assigned to their institute and study section, respectively, before you submit, and you need to refer to those people by name in your cover letter as having agreed that those assignments should be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-submission discussions with PO/SRO increase the chance of desired routing. If they agree, name them in the cover letter — Division of Receipt and Referral often follows such pre-arranged assignments, saving referral time and preventing misrouting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency-specific norms for suggesting/excluding reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Different agencies have different norms: NSF encourages submission of suggested reviewers (and reviewers to be excluded); DOE program managers may consider naming whom not to send a proposal to as bad form and prefer phone contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the specific funder's policy before including suggested reviewers or exclusion lists. What is acceptable at NSF may be counterproductive at NIH or DOE.

rubrics_metrics.name: When resubmitting after a bad review, explicitly address critiques politely and with data
rubrics_metrics.description: Address the critique head on with solid arguments and data, but do it NICE way!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a point-by-point response that corrects misunderstandings and provides additional data or experimental plans; keep tone professional and non-combative — first drafts may be angry but final responses should be constructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recusal/conflict-of-interest grounds (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Current collaboration, mentoring relationship, co-employment, marriage (mentoring relationship, co-employment and marriage are cited as default presumed COIs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These relationship types are commonly treated as conflicts and are grounds for recusal. If such relationships exist between you and a reviewer, expect recusal and consider listing the person as a conflict with an explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: You can request exclusion of a suspected biased reviewer when resubmitting
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a concern about a biased reviewer whose biases are reflected in their review comments, at least with some SROs it should be possible to exclude them on conflict grounds without knowing their identities (e.g., list 'reviewer 4' as a conflict).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call the SRO, explain why you believe a prior reviewer was biased, and request exclusion for the resubmission. Provide concrete reasons tied to relationships or behavior rather than speculation about identity when possible. Outcomes vary by SRO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals of reviews are usually futile
rubrics_metrics.description: The author: 'I’ve written a fair bit about how pointless it is to appeal the review after the fact.' Program officers may be dismissive and formal appeals rarely succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on appeals as a main strategy. Consider resubmission with strong rebuttal and revision, or pursue other mechanisms/study sections instead of expecting reversal via appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight Approach and Significance more when inferring overall impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the criterion score–overall impact score correlation data: Approach and Significance still carry the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you only have individual criterion scores, give greater weight to Approach and Significance when estimating the likely overall impact score. This can help diagnose which weaknesses sank an application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triage cutoff depends on study section scoring culture (scoring inflation varies)
rubrics_metrics.description: The impact score cutoff for triage depends very heavily on the typical scoring behavior of that study section; one section may triage in the low threes (only minor weaknesses) while another triages around five (moderate weakness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the scoring norms of the target study section. A 'good' numeric score can have different consequences across sections; strategize submission/routing accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition intensity: every element of the application must be impeccable
rubrics_metrics.description: With tight funding and many applications per cycle, everything in your grant needs to be just impeccable because one point in your impact score is the difference between life and death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish Significance, Approach, Innovation, Investigators, and Environment. Expect fierce competition and plan multiple submission strategies (different study sections, mechanisms) to increase chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume reviewer identities or exact scores from critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: You never truly know who your friends and enemies are; it is risky to assume identities from critique content. Also, individual impact scores are whole numbers and you cannot know which reviewer assigned which overall score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid basing strategy on guesses of reviewer identity. Focus on addressing the substance of critiques rather than retaliating or targeting presumed reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you must communicate reviewer exclusion/suggestion to non-NIH program managers, prefer phone contact
rubrics_metrics.description: For some agencies (DOE example), writing whom not to send the proposal to is very bad form; if you must communicate such preferences, do it only over the phone to the program manager.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate channel (phone/email/cover letter) depending on funder customs and explicit instructions. Face-to-face or phone conversations with program staff can be more effective and less risky than written lists in some agencies.
